procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated August 26, 1955, of the Election Tribunal, Patiala, in Election Petition No. 12 of 1954, declaring the two appellants' election to be void.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeal by special leave is directed against the majority judgment and order of the Election Tribunal of Patiala.

directions: The appeal is dismissed with costs to the con-testing respondents.

issue.issue_text: Whether the rejection of the nomination paper of respondent No. 18 was justified because the thumb impressions of the proposer and seconder were not properly verified according to the Election Rules.

facts: The nomination paper of respondent No. 18 was rejected by the Returning Officer because the thumb impressions of the proposer and seconder were allegedly not attested in accordance with Election Rules.
The attestation was performed by a local magistrate.
The Election Tribunal found as a matter of fact that this specific magistrate had been authorized (specified) by the Election Commission to perform such attestations.
However, there was a clerical error or 'mistake of omission' where the magistrate's name was left out of the official communication sent from the Election Commission to the local election officer.
law: The relevant Election Rule states that a person who cannot write is deemed to have signed if they place a mark on a paper in the presence of an officer specified by the Election Commission.
This specified officer must then attest the mark after being satisfied as to the person's identity.
application: The Court prioritized the factual finding of the Tribunal that the magistrate was, in reality, authorized by the Election Commission.
The Court was not persuaded by the argument that a clerical or accidental omission in the official communication could invalidate the authority that the magistrate actually possessed.
Since the magistrate was found to have been factually authorized, the attestation he performed was deemed to be legally valid and in accordance with the rules.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the rejection of the nomination paper was not justified. It held that because the magistrate who attested the thumb impressions had in fact been authorized by the Election Commission, the attestation was valid, and the clerical error of omitting his name from a communication did not render the attestation improper.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Election Tribunal was wrong in holding that there is a presumption that the improper rejection of a nomination paper materially affects the result of the election.

facts: An Election Tribunal found that a candidate's nomination paper had been improperly rejected by the Returning Officer.
The Tribunal, applying a legal presumption, held that this improper rejection materially affected the result of the election and declared the entire election void.
The appellants challenged this decision before the Supreme Court, arguing that the Tribunal was wrong to apply such a presumption.
law: Under Section 100(1)(c) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (as it stood at the time), an election could be declared void if the result was materially affected by the improper rejection of a nomination.
The Supreme Court noted that while the text of the law treated improper acceptance and improper rejection of nominations similarly, case law had established a distinction between the two.
The Court recognized a legal presumption that in cases of improper rejection of a nomination paper, the result of the election is deemed to have been materially affected.
application: The Court acknowledged the appellants' argument that the burden of proof should be on the person challenging the election to prove that the result was materially affected.

However, the Court distinguished the case of improper rejection from improper acceptance. It reasoned that it is practically impossible to demonstrate how electors would have voted if the rejected candidate had been in the race. Keeping a candidate out of the electoral arena is, by itself, a very material factor as it denies voters a choice.
In contrast, the Court noted that in cases of improper acceptance of a nomination, it is much easier to demonstrate that the presence of an extra candidate did not affect the outcome.
The Court observed that almost all Election Tribunals in the country had consistently taken the view that such a presumption exists in cases of improper rejection.
The Court also pointed to a subsequent amendment to the Act, which made improper rejection conclusive proof of a void election, as legislative sanction for this judicial interpretation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' argument and affirmed the Election Tribunal's decision. It held that there is a strong presumption that the improper rejection of a nomination paper materially affects the result of the election, and the Tribunal was correct in applying this principle.

issue.issue_text: Whether the election of the second appellant in respect of the reserved seat should not have been set aside, even if the election was found to be void.

facts: The case involved an election for a double-seat constituency, with one general seat and one reserved seat.
The Election Tribunal found that a nomination paper had been improperly rejected, which materially affected the result of the election.
The appellants argued that even if the election was void, only the general seat should be set aside, and the election of the second appellant for the reserved seat should be allowed to stand.
law: Section 100 of the relevant Act provides that if the Tribunal finds that the result of an election has been materially affected by the improper rejection of a nomination paper, the Tribunal "shall declare the election to be wholly void."
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that an election for a double-seat constituency is considered "one integral whole."
Because the election is a single, integrated event, it cannot be partially voided.
The mandate of Section 100 to declare the election "wholly void" means the entire election, including both seats, must be nullified.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that since the election for the double-seat constituency was one integral whole and the law required it to be declared "wholly void," the Tribunal was correct in setting aside the election in its entirety, including the result for the reserved seat.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the rejection of the nomination paper of respondent No. 18 was justified because the thumb impressions of the proposer and seconder were not properly verified according to the Election Rules.
appellant_arguments: A clerical or accidental mistake of omission in the communication from the Election Commission to the local election officer rendered the attestation of the thumb impressions by the magistrate unacceptable and invalid.
This mistake justified the Returning Officer's decision to reject the nomination paper.
respondent_arguments: The persons whose thumb impressions were on the nomination paper had genuinely proposed and seconded the candidate.
The magistrate who attested the thumb impressions had, as a matter of fact, been authorized by the Election Commission to do so, regardless of any clerical error in communication.
Therefore, the attestation was valid and the rejection of the nomination paper was not justified.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Election Tribunal was wrong in holding that there is a presumption that the improper rejection of a nomination paper materially affects the result of the election.
appellant_arguments: Under Section 100(1)(c), improper acceptance and improper rejection of a nomination are on the same footing.
The burden of proof is on the petitioner to establish two cumulative conditions: that the rejection was improper AND that it materially affected the election result.
Citing Vashisht Narain Sharma v. Dev Chandra and Hari Vishnu Karnath v. Syed Ahmad Ishaque, the burden of establishing both conditions lies with the person seeking to have the election set aside.
respondent_arguments: There is a strong presumption that the improper rejection of a nomination paper materially affects the result of the election.
This view is consistently held by almost all Election Tribunals in the country.
The burden lies on the person seeking to uphold the election to prove that the result was not materially affected.

It is practically impossible to demonstrate how electors would have voted if the rejected candidate had been in the race, and keeping a candidate out of the election is by itself a very material factor.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the election of the second appellant in respect of the reserved seat should not have been set aside, even if the election was found to be void.
appellant_arguments: Even if the general election was found to be void due to the improper rejection, the election for the reserved seat should have been allowed to stand.
respondent_arguments: The election for a double-seat constituency is one integral whole.
If the election is found to be void, it must be declared 'wholly void' as per Section 100, which includes both the general and the reserved seat.

cases.case_name: Chatturbhuj Vithaldas Jasani v. Moreshwar Parashram
cases.principle: The improper rejection of a nomination paper 'affects the whole election'.

cases.case_name: Karnail Singh v. Election Tribunal, Hissar
cases.principle: For the view that in the case of improper rejection of a nomination paper, there is a presumption that it has materially affected the result of the election.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In cases concerning the improper rejection of a nomination paper, there is a strong presumption that the result of the election has been materially affected, and the burden lies on the person seeking to uphold the election to prove that it was not.
obiter: While the wording of the statute places improper acceptance and improper rejection of a nomination on the same footing, case law has established a distinction between the two.
The provisions of the Evidence Act, including the rules of presumption, are applicable to the trial of an election petition.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the improper rejection of a candidate's nomination paper gives rise to a strong presumption that the result of the election has been materially affected. This presumption, consistently applied by Election Tribunals, is justified by the near impossibility for a petitioner to prove how electors would have voted for the excluded candidate. The court distinguished this from cases of improper acceptance, noting that the very act of keeping a candidate out of the electoral arena is a material factor that affects the entire election. Consequently, upon finding the rejection was improper, the Tribunal was correct to apply this presumption and, in the absence of sufficient rebuttal evidence, declare the election for the double-seat constituency "wholly void" as required by statute.
legal_tests_applied: Section 100(1)(c) of the Representation of the People Act, which states that if the Tribunal is of the opinion that the result of the election has been materially affected by the improper rejection of any nomination, it shall declare the election to be wholly void.
A legal presumption that in the case of an improper rejection of a nomination paper, the result of the election has been materially affected.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that a clerical mistake in communication from the Election Commission could invalidate an attestation, upholding the Tribunal's finding of fact that the magistrate who attested the thumb impressions was, in fact, authorized to do so.

The court held that while the statute places improper acceptance and rejection of a nomination on the same footing, case law has established a distinction, creating a presumption in cases of improper rejection that the result was materially affected. The precedents cited by the appellant were distinguished as not directly applying to a case of improper rejection.

The court refused to re-examine the evidence regarding the rebuttal of the presumption, stating that it does not ordinarily reopen findings of fact recorded by a competent Tribunal in an appeal by special leave.

The court rejected the argument to save the reserved seat, reasoning that an election for a double-seat constituency is "one integral whole" and Section 100 mandates that if an election is found to be void, it must be declared "wholly void".
why_respondent_won: The court upheld the Tribunal's finding of fact that the proposer and seconder had genuinely made the thumb impressions and that the attesting magistrate had been authorized by the Election Commission, rendering the nomination valid.

The court endorsed the view consistently taken by Election Tribunals that there is a presumption that the improper rejection of a nomination paper materially affects the result of the election, shifting the burden to the person seeking to uphold the election.

The court affirmed that under Section 100 of the Act, once the election was found to be materially affected by the improper rejection, the Tribunal was correct to declare the election "wholly void," which encompasses both the general and reserved seats in a double-seat constituency.
policy_considerations: The court recognized the "practical difficulty, almost the impossibility, of demonstrating that the electors would have cast their votes in a particular way" for a candidate who was improperly rejected.

The court reasoned that "the fact that one of several candidates for an elecion had been kept out of the arena is by itself a very material consideration," as it may have prevented electors from voting for the best or most formidable candidate available.

The court noted that a recent legislative amendment making improper rejection conclusive proof of a void election provides "legislative sanction" to the view that such rejections are fundamentally different and more serious than improper acceptances.
